Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forester
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Proximity: Physical proximity
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Vignette:
Garrett Whitfield is a 54-year-old married forester who has spent the better part of three decades working the timber stands and wilderness corridors of the Pacific Northwest. He presented for his first psychological intake in late autumn, referred by his company's occupational health programme after a supervisor noted a marked deterioration in his functioning over the preceding eighteen months. He arrived quietly, answered questions in short sentences, and kept his hands folded tightly in his lap throughout the session.

Approximately nineteen months ago, Garrett was operating a felling machine in a section of mixed conifer forest when a younger crew member, a twenty-six-year-old named Dillon, moved into the drop zone without radio confirmation. The tree came down on a line that Garrett had calculated correctly by every standard measure, but Dillon was there, and the impact crushed his left leg from the knee down. Garrett was the first to reach him. He knelt in the slash and debris, pressing his hands against the wound while Dillon screamed, and he held that position for eleven minutes until the emergency crew arrived. The smell of fresh-cut fir and the sound of the radio crackling overhead are details he has never been able to separate from what his hands felt in those eleven minutes.

In the months that followed, Garrett continued to report for work, but something had reorganised itself inside him in ways he could not name at first. He had come to believe, with a certainty that no reassurance from his supervisor or the incident investigation had loosened, that there was something particular about him — some flaw in his judgment, some essential unreliability — that had made the event possible. The investigation had cleared him entirely, but Garrett found the finding almost beside the point. He could not square it with what he knew, which was that Dillon's leg was gone below the knee and that Garrett had been the one holding the controls. He no longer trusted himself to make the calculations that had once been as natural to him as breathing, and on days when he was assigned to felling operations, he would check and recheck his work in ways that slowed the crew and left him exhausted before noon.

The triggers came with a logic that was hard to escape in his line of work. When he bumped his shin against a log skidder or strained his shoulder hauling cable — ordinary occupational pain — his body would respond as though he were back on his knees in the slash, and he would feel the pressure of Dillon's wound against his palms with a physical immediacy that made him pull his hands away from whatever he was holding. Photographs of Dillon circulated on the crew's group chat in the way they do among people who work closely together, birthday posts and fishing pictures, and each one landed on Garrett like something blunt. He had stopped opening the chat. When fieldwork required him to work in close quarters with other crew members — sharing a truck cab, walking a narrow trail side by side — he found himself acutely aware of their proximity in a way he could not explain to himself as rational, and he would manoeuvre to put distance between them.

At home, his wife Renee described him as somewhere else even when he was sitting across the dinner table. He was unable to settle into the evenings the way he once had, and he had not slept a full night in months. When strangers approached him in the hardware store or at the fuel station, something in him would sharpen and pull back. He watched people — their hands, their trajectories — in ways he recognised as excessive but could not stop. When the memories came, they came with his body: his knees would ache, his palms would press together, and alongside the physical sensation would arrive a grief so total it felt like drowning, and sometimes a rage whose object he could not clearly identify.

What finally brought Garrett to seek help was a moment three weeks before his intake. He had been asked to train a new crew member on felling procedures and had stood at the tree line for forty minutes, unable to begin. He drove home without telling anyone. He told the intake clinician that he was not sure he was still a forester. What he was most afraid of, he said, was that the answer was no.
